But if you think you know the story behind those colors, you might be falling for one of the most successful marketing myths in history. It’s been slapped on everything from the legendary Model T to the modern-day F-150, serving as a stamp of American industrial might for over a century. But where did it actually come from? Is that really Henry Ford’s signature on the grille, or just a clever bit of branding? There’s a long-standing myth in car circles that the Ford logo is a direct scan of Henry Ford’s own handwriting. description: Honda’s a household name here in the States—you see their cars, bikes, and lawnmowers just about everywhere. But what a lot of folks don’t know is that it’s a classic Japanese surname, with deep ties to the country’s agricultural roots. Written in Japanese as 本田, the name breaks down into two characters: hon, which means "root," "origin," or "base," and da, which translates to "rice field." Way back in the Heian period (think 794 to 1185 AD), surnames were usually tied to the land—so "Honda" probably referred to someone who lived near the main rice fields in their village. Makes sense, right?

description: In Japanese, “Subaru” (スバル) means “unite” or “gather together.” It’s a nice, low-key name that gets right to the brand’s heart—harmony and connection. But most people, don’t know there’s a starry backstory to it, too. Notice how the six stars are arranged in a pattern that closely mimics the actual Pleiades cluster shown here. The name wasn’t picked by chance—it’s a shout-out to the Pleiades star cluster, the group of stars that’s fascinated people for thousands of years. Over time, there have also been some interesting theories floating around the web about what the “T” symbol might represent, including the idea that it resembles a cat’s nose. While those guesses have made the logo even more memorable, they are not the most widely accepted explanation. description: The Toyota brand takes its name from founder Kiichiro Toyoda. But the company wasn’t always called Toyota. When its automotive division first launched in 1933, it used the family name: Toyoda. In July 1936, the company held a public logo contest to mark its first passenger car and build visibility. Out of 27,000 submissions, a circular design featuring the Japanese characters for “Toyota” (トヨタ) won.
